claim: Missense mutations in the p53 DNA-binding domain (DBD) contribute to half of new cancer cases annually.
source: Missense mutations in the p53 DNA-binding domain (DBD) contribute to half of new cancer cases annually.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that is based on established knowledge about p53's role in cancer.

claim: DBD possesses one of the highest zinc affinities of any eukaryotic protein.
source: We find that DBD possesses two unusual properties—one of the highest zinc affinities of any eukaryotic protein and extreme instability in the absence of zinc—which are predicted to poise p53 on the cusp of folding/unfolding in the cell, with a major determinant being available zinc concentration.
evidence: This claim is supported by direct measurements of KZn reported in the manuscript (Figure 2A) and comparison to literature values (Kochańczyk et al., 2015).

claim: DBD exhibits extreme instability in the absence of zinc.
source: We find that DBD possesses two unusual properties—one of the highest zinc affinities of any eukaryotic protein and extreme instability in the absence of zinc—which are predicted to poise p53 on the cusp of folding/unfolding in the cell, with a major determinant being available zinc concentration.
evidence: This is supported by thermodynamic measurements showing positive ΔGapo at 37°C (Figure 2D).

claim: 80% of the 20 most common tumorigenic p53 mutations impair zinc affinity, thermodynamic stability, or both.
source: We analyze the 20 most common tumorigenic p53 mutations and find that 80% impair zinc affinity, thermodynamic stability, or both.
evidence: This is based on biophysical characterization of 22 mutants presented in Figure 3C and Figure 3—source data 1.

claim: A synthetic zinc metallochaperone rescues mutations that decrease zinc affinity.
source: Biophysical, cell-based, and murine xenograft experiments demonstrate that a synthetic zinc metallochaperone rescues not only mutations that decrease zinc affinity, but also mutations that destabilize DBD without impairing zinc binding.
evidence: This is demonstrated through cell viability assays (Figure 5, Table 1), immunofluorescence (Figure 6A), and xenograft experiments (Figure 9).

claim: A synthetic zinc metallochaperone rescues mutations that destabilize DBD without impairing zinc binding.
source: Biophysical, cell-based, and murine xenograft experiments demonstrate that a synthetic zinc metallochaperone rescues not only mutations that decrease zinc affinity, but also mutations that destabilize DBD without impairing zinc binding.
evidence: This is demonstrated for stability-class mutants like V272M and Y234A in cell-based assays (Table 1, Figure 6A) and xenograft experiments (Figure 9).

claim: Zinc metallochaperones have the capability to treat 120,500 patients annually in the U.S.
source: The results suggest that zinc metallochaperones have the capability to treat 120,500 patients annually in the U.S.
evidence: This is an inference based on the frequency of rescuable mutations and cancer incidence data (Siegel et al., 2020).

claim: p53 regulates cellular responses to damage and distress.
source: The transcription factor p53 regulates a host of cellular responses to damage and distress (Kruiswijk et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: p53 can halt cell cycle progression, upregulate DNA repair pathways, and induce apoptosis.
source: Its abilities to halt cell cycle progression, upregulate DNA repair pathways, and induce apoptosis help prevent deleterious mutations from propagating in cell populations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about p53 function.

claim: Mutations in p53 are an established driver of human cancer.
source: Mutations in p53 are an established driver of human cancer (Bouaoun et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Tumorigenic alterations in p53 are overwhelmingly missense and map to nearly every position within the DNA-binding domain.
source: The mutational spectrum of p53 is atypical because tumorigenic alterations are overwhelmingly missense and map to nearly every position within one of the domains of the protein (the DNA-binding domain, or DBD) (Baugh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to mutation database analysis.

claim: Other frequently-mutated tumor suppressors such as BRCA1/2, retinoblastoma 1, and PTEN are found with mostly nonsense, deletion, or insertion mutations.
source: By contrast, other frequently-mutated tumor suppressors such as BRCA1/2 (ARUP Scientific Resource, 2020), retinoblastoma 1 (LOVD Gene homepage, 2018), and PTEN, 2020 are found with mostly nonsense, deletion, or insertion mutations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to mutation databases.

claim: p53 DBD is marked by low thermodynamic and kinetic stability.
source: From a structural standpoint, p53 DBD is unusual in that it is marked by low thermodynamic and kinetic stability (Joerger and Fersht, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The apparent melting temperature (Tm) of wild-type DBD has been measured to be 32–45°C depending on buffer composition.
source: The apparent melting temperature (Tm) of wild-type (WT) DBD has been measured to be 32–45°C depending on buffer composition (Bell et al., 2002; Butler and Loh, 2006; Friedler et al., 2003), and the protein unfolds with a half-time of 9 m at 37°C (Friedler et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental measurements.

claim: Wild-type DBD unfolds with a half-time of 9 minutes at 37°C.
source: The apparent melting temperature (Tm) of wild-type (WT) DBD has been measured to be 32–45°C depending on buffer composition (Bell et al., 2002; Butler and Loh, 2006; Friedler et al., 2003), and the protein unfolds with a half-time of 9 m at 37°C (Friedler et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous kinetic measurements.

claim: Many tumorigenic mutations reduce Tm below body temperature and/or increase the rate at which the protein unfolds.
source: As a result of this borderline stability, many tumorigenic mutations reduce Tm below body temperature and/or increase the rate at which the protein unfolds (Butler and Loh, 2006; Friedler et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies of mutant p53.

claim: p53 DBD consists of residues 94–312.
source: The X-ray crystal structure of DBD (residues 94–312) reveals a β-sandwich with a DNA-binding surface consisting of a loop-sheet-helix motif and two loops (L2 and L3) (Figure 1; Cho et al., 1994).
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure cited.

claim: DBD structure reveals a β-sandwich with a DNA-binding surface consisting of a loop-sheet-helix motif and two loops (L2 and L3).
source: The X-ray crystal structure of DBD (residues 94–312) reveals a β-sandwich with a DNA-binding surface consisting of a loop-sheet-helix motif and two loops (L2 and L3) (Figure 1; Cho et al., 1994).
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure (PDB 1TSR) shown in Figure 1.

claim: The L2 and L3 loops are stabilized by the tetrahedral coordination of a single zinc ion by C176, H179, C238, and C242.
source: These loops are stabilized by the tetrahedral coordination of a single zinc ion by C176 and H179 of L2 and C238 and C242 of L3.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure and is established knowledge.

claim: Removing Zn2+ from DBD causes loss of DNA-binding specificity.
source: Removing Zn2+ from DBD causes loss of DNA-binding specificity, widespread changes in the protein NMR spectrum, and a reduction of ~3 kcal mol−1 in the apparent folding free energy (Butler and Loh, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Removing Zn2+ from DBD causes widespread changes in the protein NMR spectrum.
source: Removing Zn2+ from DBD causes loss of DNA-binding specificity, widespread changes in the protein NMR spectrum, and a reduction of ~3 kcal mol−1 in the apparent folding free energy (Butler and Loh, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Removing Zn2+ from DBD causes a reduction of ~3 kcal mol−1 in the apparent folding free energy.
source: Removing Zn2+ from DBD causes loss of DNA-binding specificity, widespread changes in the protein NMR spectrum, and a reduction of ~3 kcal mol−1 in the apparent folding free energy (Butler and Loh, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Overexpressing Zn2+-chelating proteins causes reversible loss of sequence-specific DNA-binding activity of p53.
source: This inherent malleability has also been demonstrated in cells by overexpressing Zn2+-chelating proteins (metallothioneins) or adding small-molecule Zn2+ chelators, and observing reversible loss of sequence-specific DNA-binding activity and a switch in recognition by an antibody that recognizes native p53 (PAB1620) to one that binds to unfolded/misfolded p53 (PAB240) (Méplan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous cell-based experiments.

claim: Overexpressing Zn2+-chelating proteins causes a switch in antibody recognition from PAB1620 (native p53) to PAB240 (unfolded/misfolded p53).
source: This inherent malleability has also been demonstrated in cells by overexpressing Zn2+-chelating proteins (metallothioneins) or adding small-molecule Zn2+ chelators, and observing reversible loss of sequence-specific DNA-binding activity and a switch in recognition by an antibody that recognizes native p53 (PAB1620) to one that binds to unfolded/misfolded p53 (PAB240) (Méplan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous cell-based experiments.

claim: Many tumorigenic mutations occur in and around the zinc-binding site.
source: Many tumorigenic mutations occur in and around the zinc-binding site and presumably impair this interaction.
evidence: This is supported by the structural analysis shown in Figure 1 and the biophysical data in Figure 3C.

claim: R175H is the most common p53 mutation in cancer.
source: The most common p53 mutation in cancer, R175H, is immediately adjacent to the zinc-chelating residue C176 (Figure 1) and dramatically weakens metal-binding affinity (Butler and Loh, 2003; Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on mutation frequency data and is established knowledge.

claim: R175H is immediately adjacent to the zinc-chelating residue C176.
source: The most common p53 mutation in cancer, R175H, is immediately adjacent to the zinc-chelating residue C176 (Figure 1) and dramatically weakens metal-binding affinity (Butler and Loh, 2003; Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure (Figure 1).

claim: R175H dramatically weakens metal-binding affinity.
source: The most common p53 mutation in cancer, R175H, is immediately adjacent to the zinc-chelating residue C176 (Figure 1) and dramatically weakens metal-binding affinity (Butler and Loh, 2003; Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous measurements and confirmed by data in Figure 3C.

claim: Some cancers inactivate p53 by upregulating metallothioneins and starving wild-type p53 of zinc.
source: Furthermore, there is evidence that some cancers inactivate p53 by upregulating metallothioneins and starving wild-type (WT) p53 of zinc (Mehrian-Shai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Zinc metallochaperones reactivate mutant p53 by shuttling Zn2+ from extracellular sources through the plasma membrane and into cells.
source: By our definition, zinc metallochaperones (ZMCs) reactivate mutant p53 by shuttling Zn2+ from extracellular sources through the plasma membrane and into cells, thereby increasing intracellular Zn2+ concentrations to levels high enough to remetallate mutant p53.
evidence: This is the authors' definition and proposed mechanism.

claim: ZMCs have proven effective for multiple mutants in cell culture and mouse models of cancer.
source: This approach has proven effective for multiple mutants in cell culture and mouse models of cancer (Yu et al., 2014; Blanden et al., 2015; Garufi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and data in the current manuscript (Figures 5-9).

claim: Previous attempts to characterize DBD folding thermodynamics lack information regarding zinc-binding affinity of folded and unfolded states.
source: Previous attempts to characterize DBD folding thermodynamics have yielded valuable insight into mechanisms of p53 dysfunction, and have informed drug development efforts, but are ultimately incomplete because they lack information regarding zinc-binding affinity of folded and unfolded states (Bullock et al., 2000; Bullock et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a critique of previous work supported by citations.

claim: There is disagreement in the literature regarding which mutants are potentially treatable using zinc-based therapies.
source: Furthermore, there is disagreement in the literature regarding which mutants are potentially treatable using zinc-based therapies, likely because of the difficulty of inferring physical mechanisms from complex biological data and lack of a consensus definition regarding what constitutes a zinc-binding mutant (Garufi et al., 2013; Salim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations showing conflicting results in the literature.

claim: ΔGapo of wild-type DBD is extremely unfavorable at 37°C, indicating that wild-type DBD is intrinsically unfolded in the absence of zinc.
source: The data reveal for the first time that: (i) ΔGapo is extremely unfavorable at 37°C, indicating that wild-type (WT) DBD is intrinsically unfolded in the absence of zinc
evidence: This is based on thermodynamic measurements extrapolated to 37°C (Figure 2D).

claim: DBD has one of the highest zinc-binding affinities of any eukaryotic protein yet reported.
source: The data reveal for the first time that: (i) ΔGapo is extremely unfavorable at 37°C, indicating that wild-type (WT) DBD is intrinsically unfolded in the absence of zinc, and (ii) DBD has one of the highest zinc-binding affinities of any eukaryotic protein yet reported (Kochańczyk et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on direct measurement of KZn (Figure 2A) and comparison to literature values.

claim: The unusually large unfavorable value of ΔGapo and the atypically large favorable value of ΔGZn are predicted to nearly cancel each other out at physiological temperature and intracellular zinc concentration.
source: Remarkably, the unusually large unfavorable value of ΔGapo and the atypically large favorable value of ΔGZn are predicted to nearly cancel each other out at physiological temperature and intracellular zinc concentration, causing the overall free energy change of folding to be near zero.
evidence: This is based on the thermodynamic model and energy landscape calculations shown in Figure 3A.

claim: p53 is poised between folded and unfolded conformations in the cell, with available zinc concentration being a major determining factor.
source: Although p53's instability at 37°C has been previously documented, our modeling emphasizes that p53 is poised between folded and unfolded conformations in the cell, with available zinc concentration being a major determining factor.
evidence: This is an inference from the thermodynamic model (Figure 3A) and supported by immunoprecipitation data (Figure 10).

claim: Mutations that decrease protein stability and mutations that decrease zinc-binding affinity both cause p53 to lose function by a common unfolding mechanism.
source: It further holds that mutations that decrease protein stability (but not zinc-binding affinity) and mutations that decrease zinc-binding affinity (but not protein stability) both cause p53 to lose function by a common unfolding mechanism, and both might be similarly rescued by increasing the concentration of available Zn2+.
evidence: This is a prediction from the thermodynamic model that is tested experimentally.

claim: Both stability-class and zinc-binding-class mutants might be rescued by increasing the concentration of available Zn2+.
source: It further holds that mutations that decrease protein stability (but not zinc-binding affinity) and mutations that decrease zinc-binding affinity (but not protein stability) both cause p53 to lose function by a common unfolding mechanism, and both might be similarly rescued by increasing the concentration of available Zn2+.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model that is validated by cell-based and xenograft experiments (Figures 5-9).

claim: 22 of the most prevalent cancer-associated p53 variants were classified into three classes—stability, zinc-binding, or DNA-binding—based on ΔGapo, KZn, and KDNA.
source: As a test, we apply the model to 22 of the most prevalent cancer-associated p53 variants and classify them into three classes—stability, zinc-binding, or DNA-binding—based on (respectively) ΔGapo, KZn, and KDNA, the latter being dissociation constants for binding to a panel of p53 recognition elements.
evidence: This is based on biophysical measurements shown in Figures 3C and 4.

claim: ZMC1 reactivates members of the stability class of p53 mutants in cells.
source: We validate the model by testing whether ZMC1 reactivates members of the stability class of p53 mutants in cells, a category not previously regarded as being amenable to Zn2+ therapy.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell viability assays (Table 1), immunofluorescence (Figure 6A), and xenograft experiments (Figure 9).

claim: WT DBD binds Zn2+ with KZn = (1.6 ± 0.3) x 10−15 M at 10°C.
source: Fitting the data to the one-site binding equation yields KZn = (1.6 ± 0.3) x 10−15 M.
evidence: This is directly measured by Tyr fluorescence assay shown in Figure 2A.

claim: This is one of the lowest KZn values ever reported, with only one other eukaryotic protein possessing comparable affinity (PDZ and LIM domain protein 1; KZn = 3.2×10−15 M).
source: To our knowledge, this is one of the lowest KZn values ever reported, with only one other eukaryotic protein possessing comparable affinity (PDZ and LIM domain protein 1; KZn = 3.2×10−15 M) (Kochańczyk et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on comparison to literature values.

claim: Full-length p53 binds zinc with KZn = (0.4 ± 0.1) x 10−15 M and Hill coefficient n = 0.99 ± 0.02.
source: Fitting the data to the Hill-binding equation reveals KZn = (0.4 ± 0.1) x 10−15 M and n = 0.99 ± 0.02, indicating that each monomer binds zinc independently and that the isolated DBD is an accurate representation of the DBD in the full-length p53 tetramer.
evidence: This is directly measured by Tyr fluorescence assay shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Each monomer of the p53 tetramer binds zinc independently.
source: Fitting the data to the Hill-binding equation reveals KZn = (0.4 ± 0.1) x 10−15 M and n = 0.99 ± 0.02, indicating that each monomer binds zinc independently and that the isolated DBD is an accurate representation of the DBD in the full-length p53 tetramer.
evidence: This is inferred from the Hill coefficient being approximately 1.

claim: The isolated DBD is an accurate representation of the DBD in the full-length p53 tetramer.
source: Fitting the data to the Hill-binding equation reveals KZn = (0.4 ± 0.1) x 10−15 M and n = 0.99 ± 0.02, indicating that each monomer binds zinc independently and that the isolated DBD is an accurate representation of the DBD in the full-length p53 tetramer.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar KZn values and lack of cooperativity.

claim: Unfolded WT DBD binds zinc with KZn,U = (42 ± 7) x 10−9 M.
source: We then measured KZn,U by competition assay between urea-denatured apoDBD and the fluorescent Zn2+ chelator FluoZin-3 (Figure 2B). The apparent KZn,U value of (42 ± 7) x 10−9 M is 107-fold weaker than KZn.
evidence: This is measured by FluoZin-3 competition assay shown in Figure 2B.

claim: KZn,U of unfolded WT DBD is 107-fold weaker than KZn.
source: The apparent KZn,U value of (42 ± 7) x 10−9 M is 107-fold weaker than KZn.
evidence: This is calculated from the measured KZn and KZn,U values.

claim: C176S mutant has KZn,U = (50 ± 23) x 10−9 M, essentially identical to WT.
source: We generated a Ser mutant of the zinc-binding residue C176 and found its KZn,U to be essentially identical ((50 ± 23) x 10−9 M), indicating that the zinc-binding sites in the native and unfolded proteins are distinct (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is measured by FluoZin-3 competition assay shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The zinc-binding sites in the native and unfolded proteins are distinct.
source: We generated a Ser mutant of the zinc-binding residue C176 and found its KZn,U to be essentially identical ((50 ± 23) x 10−9 M), indicating that the zinc-binding sites in the native and unfolded proteins are distinct (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mutating a native zinc ligand does not affect KZn,U.

claim: R175H is a pure zinc-binding-class mutant.
source: Plotting folding free energy of DBD vs. [Zn2+]free (10°C) reveals that R175H (green) is a pure zinc-binding-class mutant whereas A138V (red) is a pure stability-class mutant.
evidence: This is shown by the shifted deflection point in Figure 2C.

claim: A138V is a pure stability-class mutant.
source: Plotting folding free energy of DBD vs. [Zn2+]free (10°C) reveals that R175H (green) is a pure zinc-binding-class mutant whereas A138V (red) is a pure stability-class mutant.
evidence: This is shown by the lower y-intercept in Figure 2C.

claim: Temperature dependence of apoDBD folding free energy yields ΔHm = 171 ± 20 kcal mol−1, Tm = 300 ± 1 K, and ΔCp = 7.0 ± 1.7 kcal mol−1 K−1.
source: Temperature dependence of apoDBD folding free energy fit to the Gibbs-Helmholtz equation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) yields ΔHm = 171 ± 20 kcal mol−1, Tm = 300 ± 1 K, and ΔCp = 7.0 ± 1.7 kcal mol−1 K−1 (fit value ± SE of fit).
evidence: This is obtained by fitting temperature-dependent stability data to the Gibbs-Helmholtz equation (Figure 2D).

claim: At 10°C, WT apoDBD is stable even without zinc (ΔGapo = −6.3 kcal mol−1).
source: When the protein is kept cool (10°C) it is stable even without zinc (ΔGapo = −6.3 kcal mol−1; Figure 2D), making Fholo effectively unity at all relevant concentrations of free zinc (>10−15 M; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D and Figure 3A.

claim: At 37°C, WT apoDBD is completely unfolded without zinc (ΔGapo = 6.9 kcal mol−1).
source: At 37°C, however, the protein is completely unfolded without zinc (ΔGapo = 6.9 kcal mol−1).
evidence: This is extrapolated from temperature-dependent measurements using the Gibbs-Helmholtz equation.

claim: At 37°C and 10−10 M free zinc, WT p53 has Fholo = 0.43.
source: Strikingly, the high zinc-binding affinity of WT apoDBD together with the concentration of free zinc in the typical cell (10−10 M) (Krezel and Maret, 2006; Vinkenborg et al., 2009) result in an overall ΔGfold near zero and Fholo = 0.43 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is calculated from the energy landscape model shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Under normal physiological conditions, WT p53 is balanced on the edge of folding and unfolding.
source: This suggests that under normal physiological conditions, WT p53 is balanced on the edge of folding and unfolding and may be pushed in either direction by surprisingly small changes in [Zn2+]free, ΔGapo, KZn, or temperature.
evidence: This is inferred from the energy landscape calculations.

claim: Raising [Zn2+]free to 10−9 M yields Fholo = 0.9.
source: For example, raising [Zn2+]free to 10−9 M or lowering it to 10−11 M yields Fholo values of 0.9 and 0.08, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from the energy landscape model.

claim: Lowering [Zn2+]free to 10−11 M yields Fholo = 0.08.
source: For example, raising [Zn2+]free to 10−9 M or lowering it to 10−11 M yields Fholo values of 0.9 and 0.08, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from the energy landscape model.

claim: At 10°C, ΔGholo,theory (−12.3 kcal mol−1) and ΔGholo (−10.6 kcal mol−1) are in good agreement.
source: At 10°C, where ΔGapo and ΔGholo are both determined experimentally, ΔGholo,theory (−12.3 kcal mol−1) and ΔGholo (−10.6 kcal mol−1) are in good agreement.
evidence: This validates the model by comparing to previous measurements by Fersht and coworkers.

claim: At 37°C, ΔGholo,theory and ΔGholo are nearly identical (−2.9 kcal mol−1 and −3.0 kcal mol−1, respectively).
source: At 37°C, where ΔGapo and ΔGholo are extrapolated values, ΔGholo,theory and ΔGholo are nearly identical (−2.9 kcal mol−1 and −3.0 kcal mol−1, respectively).
evidence: This validates the extrapolation by comparing to previous measurements by Fersht and coworkers.

claim: The ΔCp value obtained is substantially higher than the figure calculated based on the change in accessible surface area of holoDBD upon unfolding (3.8 kcal mol−1 K−1).
source: We note, however, that the ΔCp value we obtain is substantially higher than the figure calculated based on the change in accessible surface area of holoDBD upon unfolding (3.8 kcal mol−1 K−1) (Bullock et al., 2000; Myers et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a comparison to theoretical predictions from structure.

claim: apoDBD possesses a stability that is unusually dependent on temperature owing to its large ΔCp value.
source: We therefore conclude that apoDBD, owing to its large ΔCp value, possesses a stability that is unusually dependent on temperature.
evidence: This is inferred from the measured ΔCp value.

claim: 17 of the top 20 most common tumorigenic p53 mutations impair DBD thermodynamic stability, zinc-binding affinity, or both.
source: Of the 22 most common tumorigenic mutations examined here, all but three reduce stability by >1 kcal mol−1, decrease Zn2+ binding affinity by >10 fold, or both. The remaining three belong to the DNA-contact class.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and summarized in the text.

claim: Pure zinc-binding mutants exhibit decreased Zn2+ affinity but normal stability.
source: Pure zinc-binding mutants exhibit decreased Zn2+ affinity but normal stability and thus cluster near a vertical line drawn directly below WT DBD (green box).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Members of the zinc-binding class include R175H, C176S, C242S, and H179R.
source: Members of this class include R175H as well as the direct Zn2+ ligating mutants C176S, C242S, and H179R.
evidence: This is based on the classification shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The analysis reveals a number zinc-binding mutations (P152L, L194F, R282Q) that were not previously suspected due to their long distances from the metal-binding pocket.
source: Significantly, the analysis reveals a number zinc-binding mutations (P152L, L194F, R282Q) that were not previously suspected as being so due to their long distances from the metal-binding pocket (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on the classification in Figure 3C and structural analysis in Figure 1.

claim: Pure stability mutants are less stable than WT but suffer no zinc-binding deficiency.
source: Pure stability mutants are less stable than WT but suffer no zinc-binding deficiency; these are defined by falling near the horizontal line drawn to the left of WT DBD (red box in Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Destabilizing WT apoDBD using sub-denaturing amounts of urea does not affect KZn.
source: To validate that protein stability can indeed be separated from zinc affinity in this manner, we destabilized WT apoDBD using sub-denaturing amounts of urea and measured KZn using the Tyr fluorescence assay. These data (open circles) fall on the horizontal line as predicted by the model.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C (open circles).

claim: The mixed-phenotype mutants (A138V, V267F, R158H, M237I) decrease both stability and zinc affinity.
source: The mixed-phenotype mutants (A138V, V267F, R158H, M237I; orange box in Figure 3C) decrease both stability and zinc affinity.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Only three mutations (R248Q, R273H, R280K) do not impair stability or metal affinity.
source: Only three mutations (R248Q, R273H, R280K) do not impair stability or metal affinity (blue box in Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: R248Q, R273H, and R280K residues are in direct contact with DNA.
source: These residues are in direct contact with DNA (Figure 1).
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure (Figure 1).

claim: DNA-contact mutants are more stable than WT, likely because they remove or reposition a positive charge and reduce repulsions in the highly cationic DNA-binding groove.
source: DNA-contact mutants are more stable than WT, likely because they remove or reposition a positive charge and reduce repulsions in the highly cationic DNA-binding groove (Butler and Loh, 2003; Bullock et al., 2000).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citations.

claim: DNA-contact mutants bind zinc normally.
source: Our data confirm that they bind zinc normally and have lost DNA-binding affinity (vide infra).
evidence: This is confirmed by the data in Figure 3C and Figure 4.

claim: The most severe stability-class mutant reduces ΔGapo by 4.6 kcal mol−1 (E285K).
source: The most severe member of each class reduces ΔGapo by 4.6 kcal mol−1 (E285K) and KZn by 5 orders of magnitude (C176S).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—source data 1.

claim: The most severe zinc-binding-class mutant reduces KZn by 5 orders of magnitude (C176S).
source: The most severe member of each class reduces ΔGapo by 4.6 kcal mol−1 (E285K) and KZn by 5 orders of magnitude (C176S).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—source data 1.

claim: Several zinc-binding or mixed mutations (L194F, R282Q, V157F, R158H, P152L) lie far from the canonical zinc-binding pocket, suggesting long-range communication between distant regions of DBD.
source: Additionally, several zinc-binding or mixed mutations (L194F, R282Q, V157F, R158H, P152L) lie far from the canonical zinc-binding pocket, suggesting long-range communication between distant regions of DBD.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural locations shown in Figure 1 and the biophysical data in Figure 3C.

claim: Adjacent mutations can produce markedly different effects.
source: The subtle nature of DBD structure and energetics is also evident from the observation that adjacent mutations can produce markedly different effects. For example, R248Q is a classic DNA-contact mutant whereas R249S is a pure zinc-binding mutant.
evidence: This is shown by comparing R248Q and R249S in Figure 3C.

claim: R248Q is a classic DNA-contact mutant whereas R249S is a pure zinc-binding mutant.
source: For example, R248Q is a classic DNA-contact mutant whereas R249S is a pure zinc-binding mutant.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Most of the stability and mixed mutants maintain similar binding affinity for the different p53REs.
source: By visual inspection, most of the stability and mixed mutants maintain similar binding affinity for the different p53REs, whereas all of the DNA-contact mutants and most of the zinc-binding mutants lose measurable affinity for all p53REs (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown in the heat map in Figure 4.

claim: All of the DNA-contact mutants and most of the zinc-binding mutants lose measurable affinity for all p53REs.
source: By visual inspection, most of the stability and mixed mutants maintain similar binding affinity for the different p53REs, whereas all of the DNA-contact mutants and most of the zinc-binding mutants lose measurable affinity for all p53REs (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown in the heat map in Figure 4.

claim: The majority of zinc-binding mutants purify with sub-stoichiometric but detectable zinc content.
source: The majority of zinc-binding mutants purify with sub-stoichiometric but detectable zinc content (e.g. R175H contains 0.6 equivalents of Zn2+ 14), and consequently should show partial DNA-binding activity.
evidence: This is based on previous measurements cited in the text.

claim: Loss of DNA-binding in zinc-binding mutants may be caused by Zn2+ misligating to non-native sites.

claim: Zinc-induced stabilization takes advantage of an existing high-affinity site on p53 (KZn ~ 10−15 M) and can in principle refold any stability-class mutant.
source: Zinc-induced stabilization, by contrast, takes advantage of an existing high-affinity site on p53 (KZn ~ 10−15 M) and can in principle refold any stability-class mutant, but suffers from lack of bio-orthogonality.
evidence: This is based on the thermodynamic model and experimental data.

claim: Treating cells with ZMC1 reactivated three stability-class mutants in cells (Y234A, V272M, and G245S) and in vivo (V272M).
source: As evidence for the potential breadth of ZMC therapy, treating cells with ZMC1 reactivated three stability-class mutants in cells (Y234A, V272M, and G245S [Yu et al., 2014]) and in vivo (V272M), failed to reactivate two (Y234C and E285K).
evidence: This is based on the current data and previous studies cited.

claim: ZMC1 failed to reactivate Y234C and E285K.
source: As evidence for the potential breadth of ZMC therapy, treating cells with ZMC1 reactivated three stability-class mutants in cells (Y234A, V272M, and G245S [Yu et al., 2014]) and in vivo (V272M), failed to reactivate two (Y234C and E285K).
evidence: This is shown in the cell-based and xenograft data.

claim: Y234C is refractory to zinc-induced stabilization most likely because of metal misligation in unfolded or partially folded states.
source: Y234C, like all the Tyr→Cys mutants that we tested, is refractory to zinc-induced stabilization most likely because of metal misligation in unfolded or partially folded states.
evidence: This is inferred from the KZn,U measurements.

claim: E285K is the most unstable variant characterized, which may explain why elevated zinc alone was insufficient for refolding without the additional stabilizing factor of reduced temperature.
source: E285K is the most unstable variant that we have characterized, which may explain why elevated zinc alone was insufficient for refolding without the additional stabilizing factor of reduced temperature.
evidence: This is inferred from the stability measurements and temperature-dependent refolding data.

claim: The discovery that ZMCs can reactivate mutants beyond just the class of zinc deficient mutation is a significant finding.
source: Nonetheless, the discovery that ZMC's can reactivate mutants beyond just the class of zinc deficient mutation is a significant finding.
evidence: This is the authors' assessment of the significance of their findings.

claim: In the absence of zinc, WT apoDBD is much more unfolded than previously thought at body temperature (ΔGapo = 6.9 kcal mol−1).
source: In the absence of zinc, we find that WT apoDBD is much more unfolded than previously thought at body temperature (ΔGapo = 6.9 kcal mol−1).
evidence: This is based on extrapolation of temperature-dependent stability measurements.

claim: DBD achieves instability at 37°C by a unique mechanism involving anomalously high dependence of ΔGapo on temperature.
source: This is not due to DBD being intrinsically disordered—it is quite stable at 10°C—but to the anomalously high dependence of ΔGapo on temperature.
evidence: This is inferred from the large ΔCp value measured.

claim: At typical intracellular concentrations of available Zn2+ (10−10 M), the folded and unfolded populations of p53 are comparable.
source: These biophysical data suggest that, in the absence of other cellular considerations such as chaperones and p53 binding partners, a dominant factor determining whether p53 is folded or unfolded is the available concentration of cytosolic zinc At typical intracellular concentrations of available Zn2+ (10−10 M), our modeling predicts that the folded and unfolded populations are comparable—a prediction supported by conformation-specific antibody experiments (Figure 10).
evidence: This is based on the energy landscape model and validated by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 10.

claim: The balance between folded and unfolded p53 may explain why so many different missense mutations at nearly every codon position in the DBD gene are associated with loss of p53 function and cancer.
source: This balance may explain why so many different missense mutations at nearly every codon position in the DBD gene are associated with loss of p53 function and cancer (Baugh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference from the thermodynamic model.

claim: More often than not, an amino acid substitution at any given position will decrease folding free energy rather than increase it.
source: More often than not, an amino acid substitution at any given position will decrease folding free energy rather than increase it, and loss of thermodynamic stability is the major cause of diseases that are caused by missense mutation of a single protein (Yue et al., 2005).
evidence: This is general knowledge about protein folding supported by citation.

claim: Loss of thermodynamic stability is the major cause of diseases that are caused by missense mutation of a single protein.
source: More often than not, an amino acid substitution at any given position will decrease folding free energy rather than increase it, and loss of thermodynamic stability is the major cause of diseases that are caused by missense mutation of a single protein (Yue et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Nearly all mutants examined in this study destabilize DBD and/or decrease its zinc affinity.
source: To emphasize this point, nearly all mutants examined in this study destabilize DBD and/or decrease its zinc affinity. The remainder are DNA-contact mutants, which can be reliably deduced from inspecting the X-ray crystal structure of DBD.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: DNA-contact mutants can be reliably deduced from inspecting the X-ray crystal structure of DBD.
source: The remainder are DNA-contact mutants, which can be reliably deduced from inspecting the X-ray crystal structure of DBD.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: p53's unusual combination of high instability and zinc affinity constitutes a built-in failsafe to help rein in p53's powerful cytotoxic activities should cellular checkpoint pathways become compromised.
source: Why, then, might p53 have evolved with this unusual and precarious combination of high instability and zinc affinity? One explanation is that it constitutes a built-in failsafe to help rein in p53's powerful cytotoxic activities should cellular checkpoint pathways become compromised.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary rationale.

claim: The cell can reversibly regulate p53 function by modulating its conformation through available zinc levels.
source: Carrying this scenario further, one might also speculate that it is a mechanism by which the cell can reversibly regulate p53 function by modulating its conformation through available zinc levels.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential regulatory mechanisms.

claim: Milner and Watson reported that fresh medium induced cell cycle and conformational changes in p53.
source: Evidence for conformational regulation of p53 has existed for some time. Milner and Watson reported that fresh medium induced cell cycle and conformational changes in p53 (Milner and Watson, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Incubating cells and cell lysates with metal chelators can starve p53 of Zn2+ and induce the PAB240-binding form of p53, which can be rescued by re-introducing zinc.
source: Hainaut, Milner, and colleagues reported that incubating cells and cell lysates with metal chelators can starve p53 of Zn2+ and induce the PAB240-binding form of p53, which can be rescued by re-introducing zinc (Méplan et al., 2000; Hainaut and Milner, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Oxidative agents when applied to cells can induce the PAB240 conformation in WT p53.
source: They also reported that oxidative agents when applied to cells can also induce the PAB240 conformation in WT p53.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Oxidative agents increase intracellular free zinc levels by oxidizing the zinc-binding cysteine residues on cytosolic metallothionein proteins, decreasing their affinity for zinc.
source: Oxidative agents increase intracellular free zinc levels by oxidizing the zinc-binding cysteine residues on cytosolic metallothionein proteins, decreasing their affinity for zinc (Maret, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Stress signals could modulate the relative abundance of holo and apo p53 in the cell by altering zinc affinity or intracellular zinc levels.
source: Since stress signals can regulate p53 it is also possible that similar stress signals could modulate the relative abundance of holo and apo p53 in the cell by altering zinc affinity or intracellular zinc levels.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential regulatory mechanisms.

claim: Approximately 10% of the proteins encoded by the human genome bind zinc.
source: Approximately 10% of the proteins encoded by the human genome bind zinc; however, not until the last decade have researchers discovered that cytosolic zinc levels are in the picomolar range while the total cellular zinc is in the hundreds of micromolar (Krezel and Maret, 2006) and more importantly, that many proteins are functionally regulated by zinc (Maret, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: Cytosolic zinc levels are in the picomolar range while the total cellular zinc is in the hundreds of micromolar.
source: Approximately 10% of the proteins encoded by the human genome bind zinc; however, not until the last decade have researchers discovered that cytosolic zinc levels are in the picomolar range while the total cellular zinc is in the hundreds of micromolar (Krezel and Maret, 2006) and more importantly, that many proteins are functionally regulated by zinc (Maret, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Many proteins are functionally regulated by zinc.
source: Approximately 10% of the proteins encoded by the human genome bind zinc; however, not until the last decade have researchers discovered that cytosolic zinc levels are in the picomolar range while the total cellular zinc is in the hundreds of micromolar (Krezel and Maret, 2006) and more importantly, that many proteins are functionally regulated by zinc (Maret, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Proteins such as tyrosine phosphatases are regulated by zinc and typically have zinc affinities in the range of cytosolic free zinc.
source: Proteins such tyrosine phosphatases are regulated by zinc, and these proteins typically have zinc affinities in the range of cytosolic free zinc (Wilson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The effective KZn of apoDBD at physiological temperature (KZn,eff) is orders of magnitude higher than the measured KZn owing to the inherent instability of apoDBD at 37°C.
source: Although KZn of apoDBD is extremely low (1.6 × 10−15 M), the effective KZn at physiological temperature (KZn,eff) is orders of magnitude higher owing to the inherent instability of apoDBD at 37°C.
evidence: This is inferred from the thermodynamic model.

claim: KZn,eff is approximated by the product of KZn and Kapo.
source: KZn,eff is approximated by the product of KZn and Kapo (Equation 4)—a value that our modeling suggests is close to cytosolic [Zn2+]free (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on the thermodynamic model.

claim: Physiologic perturbations in cytosolic zinc levels (100's of pM) could in theory modulate zinc binding to p53 and hence its function.
source: This suggests that physiologic perturbations in cytosolic zinc levels (100's of pM), could in theory modulate zinc binding to p53 and hence its function.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the energy landscape model.

claim: Both apo and holo forms of WT p53 can be detected in cells.
source: Moreover, given our findings that both apo and holo forms of WT p53 can be detected in cells, this suggests that p53 could potentially be regulated conformationally by zinc.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10.

claim: p53 could potentially be regulated conformationally by zinc.
source: Moreover, given our findings that both apo and holo forms of WT p53 can be detected in cells, this suggests that p53 could potentially be regulated conformationally by zinc.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Mutations in six positions (R175, C176, H179, C242, G245, V272) are associated with new cancer cases in more than 120,000 patients each year in the U.S.
source: We have demonstrated that ZMC1 treatment rescues the function of not only zinc-binding class mutants (e.g. R175, C176, H179, C242), but also that of some stability-class mutants (e.g. G245 and V272). Mutations in these six positions alone are associated with new cancer cases in more than 120,000 patients each year in the U.S. (Siegel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on cancer incidence data cited.
